items.title: Classic triad of nephrotic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Classic triad

  • Proteinuria in the nephrotic range (>3.5 g/24h in adults, >40 mg/m²/h in children) is the cardinal finding, secondary to increased glomerular permeability.
  • Edema: initially periorbital and malleolar, progresses to anasarca; The classic mechanism is hydrosaline retention due to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, although hypoalbuminemia reduces plasma oncotic pressure.
  • Hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL) results from urinary albumin loss and increased renal catabolism.
  • The triad is completed with hyperlipidemia (elevated cholesterol and triglycerides) due to compensatory hepatic synthesis, although it is not part of the classic definition.

items.foco: Most common cause in children: minimal change nephropathy
items.title: Most common cause in children: minimal change nephropathy
items.contentHtml:
Minimal change nephropathy

  • It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (80-90% in children under 10 years of age).
  • Histology: fusion of podocytes (effacement of pedicels) in electron microscopy; Normal optical microscopy and immunofluorescence.
  • Abrupt presentation with edema and selective proteinuria (predominance of albumin).
  • Responds excellently to corticosteroids in high doses (prednisone 60 mg/m²/day or 2 mg/kg/day); most achieve remission in 4-6 weeks.
  • The prognosis is excellent, although relapses are frequent (corticoid dependent or cortico-resistant in some cases).

items.foco: Most common cause in adults: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
items.title: Most common cause in adults: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
items.contentHtml:
Segmental and focal glomerulosclerosis

  • It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults (approximately 40% of primary cases).
  • Histology: segmental sclerosis (affects part of the glomerular tuft) and focal (only some glomeruli) in light microscopy; deposits of immunoglobulin M and complement C3 in sclerotic areas.
  • It presents with non-selective proteinuria, often associated with arterial hypertension and renal failure.
  • It responds less to corticosteroids than minimal change nephropathy; requires prolonged treatment with immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, mycophenolate).
  • High rate of progression to end-stage chronic kidney disease and most common post-transplant recurrence among glomerulopathies.

items.foco: Proteinuria in the nephrotic range: >3.5 g/24h
items.title: Proteinuria in the nephrotic range
items.contentHtml:
Proteinuria in the nephrotic range

  • Definition: urinary protein excretion >3.5 g/24h in adults, or >40 mg/m²/h in children, or protein/creatinine ratio in urine >3.5 mg/mg (or >350 mg/mmol).
  • Equivalent to proteinuria. >3+ on test strip (300 mg/dL or more).
  • It is the essential criterion for the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome; without massive proteinuria the definition is not met.
  • Proteinuria is secondary to loss of the glomerular filtration barrier (podocytes, glomerular basement membrane, fenestrated endothelium).
  • In nephrotic syndrome, proteinuria is typically non-selective in secondary causes, while in minimal change nephropathy it can be selective (albumin predominance).

items.foco: Indication of renal biopsy in nephrotic syndrome
items.title: Indication for kidney biopsy
items.contentHtml:
Indication for renal biopsy

  • In adults with de novo nephrotic syndrome: renal biopsy is indicated to establish the histological diagnosis, since the primary causes are varied (segmental and focal glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, nephropathy due to minimal changes).
  • In children under 10 years of age with typical presentation (nephropathy due to minimal changes). minimal) empirical treatment with corticosteroids is started without biopsy; biopsy is performed if there is: age <1 year (rule out congenital nephrotic syndrome), macroscopic hematuria, arterial hypertension, renal failure, or lack of response to 6-8 weeks of corticosteroids.
  • Other indications: suspicion of systemic disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, amyloidosis), rapidly progressive proteinuria, or before aggressive immunosuppression.
  • Contraindications: solitary kidney, hemorrhagic diathesis, active infection not controlled.

items.foco: Complications: infections, thrombosis, acute kidney failure
items.title: Complications of nephrotic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Complications

  • Infections: increased risk due to urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement factor B; infections due to encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae) and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
  • Thrombosis: hypercoagulable state due to loss of antithrombin III, protein C and S, and increase in procoagulant factors (fibrinogen). Renal vein thrombosis is classic in membranous nephropathy; also deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
  • Acute renal failure: may be due to hypovolemia due to massive edema, acute tubular necrosis, or bilateral renal vein thrombosis.
  • Others: hypocalcemia (due to loss of protein-bound vitamin D), malnutrition, hyperlipidemia accelerating atherosclerosis.

items.title: Initial treatment with corticosteroids
items.contentHtml:
Initial treatment

  • First line: high-dose corticosteroids (prednisone or prednisolone) at 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 80 mg/day) orally for 4-6 weeks, followed by tapering.
  • In children: prednisone 60 mg/m²/day (maximum 60 mg/day) for 4-6 weeks, then every other day.
  • The response is evaluated by disappearance of proteinuria (complete remission: proteinuria <0.3 g/24h or negative test strip).
  • If there is corticosteroid resistance (lack of remission after 8 weeks of full dose), renal biopsy and change to immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, or mycophenolate mofetil are considered.
  • In membranous nephropathy specific treatment with calcineurin inhibitors or rituximab is used if there is a high risk of progression.

items.foco: Histological lesion in membranous nephropathy: thickening of the basement membrane
items.title: Histological lesion in membranous nephropathy
items.contentHtml:
Membranous nephropathy

  • Key finding in light microscopy: diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane without hypercellularity.
  • Electron microscopy: electron-dense, subepithelial deposits (between podocyte and basement membrane), with basement membrane projections (spikes) surrounding the deposits.
  • Immunofluorescence: pattern granular immunoglobulin G and complement C3 along the glomerular capillaries.
  • It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults over 60 years of age and the second overall cause in adults; associated with anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) antibodies in 70-80% of primary cases.
  • Clinically: non-selective proteinuria, edema, and high risk of renal venous thrombosis.

items.foco: Congenital nephrotic syndrome: mutation in the NPHS1 (nephrin) gene
items.title: Congenital nephrotic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Congenital nephrotic syndrome

  • Definition: nephrotic syndrome that occurs in the first 3 months of life (typically at birth or in the first weeks).
  • Most common cause: mutation in the NPHS1 gene (chromosome 19q13) that encodes nephrin, an essential protein of the filtration diaphragm podocyte.
  • Autosomal recessive inheritance; more common in the Finnish population (Finnish congenital nephrotic syndrome).
  • Clinical symptoms: massive proteinuria, severe edema, severe hypoalbuminemia, and failure to thrive; It is usually resistant to corticosteroids.
  • Treatment: initially albuminotherapy and diuretics; eventually nephrectomy and dialysis to allow kidney transplant (post-transplant recurrence is rare because the defect is intrinsic to the native kidney).

items.title: Differential diagnosis with nephritic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Differential diagnosis: nephrotic syndrome vs. nephritic

  • Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), edema, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia; without significant hematuria or arterial hypertension in the initial stages (except in segmental and focal glomerulosclerosis).
  • Nephritic syndrome: hematuria (dysmorphic, blood casts), oliguria, arterial hypertension, facial edema, subnephrotic proteinuria (<3.5 g/24h), elevated serum creatinine; typical of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, immunoglobulin A nephropathy.
  • Key fact: in nephritic syndrome proteinuria is <3.5 g/24h, while in nephrotic syndrome it is >3.5 g/24h; Furthermore, macroscopic hematuria and hypertension are much more common in nephritic patients.
  • Both can coexist (mixed nephrotic-nephritic syndrome) in certain diseases such as class IV lupus nephritis.

items.foco: Use of ACE inhibitors or ARBs for proteinuria
items.title: Use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists
items.contentHtml:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists

  • Indication: reduction of proteinuria in any nephrotic syndrome, regardless of blood pressure, as part of antiproteinuric and renoprotective treatment.
  • Mechanism: they decrease intraglomerular pressure and reduce hyperfiltration, in addition to antifibrotic effects.
  • Dose: They are titrated to the maximum tolerated dose (e.g. enalapril 10-40 mg/day, losartan 50-100 mg/day) monitoring serum potassium and creatinine.
  • It is recommended as adjuvant therapy to immunosuppressive treatment, especially in cases of persistent proteinuria or cortico-resistance.
  • Contraindications: bilateral renal artery stenosis, pregnancy, severe hyperkalemia.

items.foco: Most common post-transplant recurrence: focal glomerulosclerosis
items.title: Post-transplant recurrence: segmental and focal glomerulosclerosis
items.contentHtml:
Post-transplant recurrence

  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is the primary glomerulopathy with the highest rate of post-transplant recurrence (30-50% of cases).
  • Relapse usually occurs early (days to months after transplant) and manifests with recurrent massive proteinuria.
  • Main risk factor: aggressive primary disease that progressed to kidney disease. terminal chronic disease in less than 3 years.
  • Mechanism: presence of a circulating permeability factor (probably the soluble form of the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor, suPAR) that damages the podocytes of the graft.
  • Treatment: plasmapheresis, rituximab, or cyclophosphamide; The response is variable and the graft prognosis is worse than in other glomerulopathies.
